Les abeilles se donnent des adresses en: Bees give each other addresses by dancing.
Karl von Frisch publie sa théorie de la: Karl von Frisch published his theory of the waggle dance: the angle gives the direction, the duration gives the distance. It would earn him the Nobel Prize in 1973.
Athens entrusts its council to chance.
Clisthène crée dix tribus fondées sur le: Cleisthenes created ten tribes based on where people lived and a council of 500 citizens chosen by lot. He called it isonomia, equality before the law.
A sherd is enough to exile a man.
Les Athéniens exilent Hipparque, fils de: The Athenians exiled Hipparchus, son of Charmus, for ten years. It took 6,000 votes, carved on pieces of pottery.
Icelanders govern themselves without a king.
À Þingvellir, les chefs islandais fonden: At Þingvellir, the Icelandic chieftains founded an annual open-air assembly. A lawspeaker recited the law there, one third each summer.
Vers 1564, Cardano écrit le Liber de lud: Around 1564, Cardano wrote the Liber de ludo aleae, the first systematic study of probability. It would not be published until 1663.
A thousand trials do not lie.
L'Ars Conjectandi de Jacques Bernoulli d: Jacob Bernoulli's Ars Conjectandi proved that the observed frequency approaches the probability as trials multiply. Poisson would name the law in 1837.
Le Parlement anglais promet jusqu'à 20 0: The English Parliament promised up to £20,000 to whoever could measure longitude at sea. A carpenter, John Harrison, would win with his timekeepers.
Le premier tome de l'Encyclopédie: The first volume of the Encyclopédie
Diderot et d'Alembert publient le premie: Diderot and d'Alembert published the first of 28 volumes. More than 140 authors would contribute until 1772.
Condorcet montre qu'avec trois options,: Condorcet showed that with three options, a majority can prefer A to B, B to C and C to A. No winner.
The price knows what no one knows.
Friedrich Hayek publie « The Use of Know: Friedrich Hayek published "The Use of Knowledge in Society": knowledge is scattered among everyone, and prices gather it.
At last, a map of who likes whom.
Jacob Moreno publie Who Shall Survive?,: Jacob Moreno published Who Shall Survive?, with some of the first maps of social networks. They explain an epidemic of runaways.
Kurt Lewin, Ronald Lippitt et Ralph Whit: Kurt Lewin, Ronald Lippitt and Ralph White compared authoritarian, democratic and laissez-faire leaders. Democratic work holds when the leader is away.
Two camps are born for one trophy.
Muzafer Sherif montre qu'une compétition: Muzafer Sherif showed that competition is enough to turn two groups of boys against each other, and that a common goal reconciles them.
The building site directs the worker.
Pierre-Paul Grassé nomme la coordination: Pierre-Paul Grassé named the coordination of termites through the traces of their work. The idea would also explain ant trails.
Anonymous experts are wrong less often.
Norman Dalkey et Olaf Helmer, de la RAND: Norman Dalkey and Olaf Helmer, of RAND, published their method: anonymous questionnaires, several rounds, a summary between each.
Quelques raccourcis rapetissent le monde: A few shortcuts shrink the world.
Duncan Watts et Steven Strogatz montrent: Duncan Watts and Steven Strogatz showed in Nature that a network of neighbors, plus a few random links, makes all paths short.
Robert Axelrod publie le récit de ses to: Robert Axelrod published the account of his tournaments: tit for tat, cooperate then return the favor, beats all the cunning strategies.
Philip Tetlock et Barbara Mellers lancen: Philip Tetlock and Barbara Mellers launched a project that won the U.S. intelligence forecasting tournament: in four years, more than a million forecasts on about 500 questions.
Cinquante mille joueurs contre un champi: Fifty thousand players against one champion.
Plus de 50 000 internautes de 75 pays vo: More than 50,000 Internet users from 75 countries voted on each move against Garry Kasparov. He won in 62 moves and spoke of the greatest game in history.
Drazen Prelec et ses collègues publient: Drazen Prelec and his colleagues published in Nature a method that keeps the answer chosen more often than predicted: about 21% fewer errors than a majority vote.
